transcript.text: f/f freezer keeps icing up bottom drawer wont shut proper, defrosted it 2wks ago already full of ice again. indesit

Fast ice build-up like that almost always means warm, damp air is getting in, usually because the door isn't sealing. It's often a vicious circle: a bit of ice stops the drawer or door closing, more air gets in, and more ice forms.

## Check these first (free/easy)

1. Door seal (most likely culprit)
• Paper test: Close the door on a sheet of paper or a banknote at several points around the door, especially the bottom corners and hinge side. If it slides out easily anywhere, the seal isn't gripping there.
• Look for splits, flattened sections, or gaps, especially at the bottom corners.
• Clean the seal with warm soapy water. Sticky gunk can stop it sealing, or make it stick and tear.
• If it's just misshapen, warm it gently with a hairdryer (low heat), press it into shape, and close the door to let it set.

2. Is the fridge level?
• The front should be slightly higher than the back so the doors swing shut on their own.
• Adjust the front feet, then open the door halfway and let go. It should close itself.

3. Drawers and contents
• Make sure no drawer is cracked, warped, or sitting off its runners. One sticking out a few mm will hold the door open.
• Check that nothing (bags, ice packs) is poking out the front.
• Put the drawers back in their correct order, as they're often different sizes.

4. Door alignment
• Look at the door from the side. If it sags or isn't flush with the cabinet, the hinge may need tightening. This often happens if the doors have been reversed or the freezer gets heavy use.

## Where's the ice forming?

• Around the door edge or front of the drawers → points to the seal or door alignment.
• Thick ice on the back wall, especially if it's a "No Frost" model → points more to a defrost fault (heater, sensor, or blocked drain). That needs an engineer or replacement parts.

(Check your model number on the sticker inside the fridge section. If it says "NF" or "No Frost," it shouldn't be icing up at all.)

## Other contributors
• Thermostat set to max all the time
• Putting warm food in
• Frequent or long door openings
• Very humid room (garage, utility)

## If it's the seal
Replacement seals for Indesit usually cost £20–£50. Search your model number + "freezer door seal." They're fairly DIY-friendly: most push into a groove or are held behind screws.

Before testing, defrost it fully again and dry it thoroughly, or the leftover ice will skew the results.

Do you know if it's a No Frost model, and where the ice is mainly building up? That'll narrow it down.
not no frost, its a manual defrost one. ice is mostly round the front edge and the bottom drawer, thick frost

That pattern (thick frost at the front edge and around the bottom drawer) points strongly to the freezer door not sealing at the bottom. Damp air is getting in there and freezing on the first cold surface it hits. It's very fixable.

## 1. Defrost fully again and dry it properly
Any leftover ice behind the bottom drawer pushes it forward, which holds the door open and starts the cycle again.
• Defrost completely, then wipe everything bone dry, including the seal and the floor of the compartment.
• Run it empty for a few hours to get cold before reloading.

## 2. Check the bottom of the door seal
This is the most likely culprit.
• Paper test along the bottom edge and both bottom corners: close the door on a sheet of paper. If it pulls out with no resistance, there's a gap.
• Look closely at the bottom hinge-side corner. Seals often split or fold over there.
• If it's just flattened or twisted, warm it with a hairdryer on low, pull it gently back into shape, and shut the door to let it set.
• If it's torn or won't hold its shape, replace it. Indesit seals are easy to get using the model number on the rating plate (usually £25–50). Most just push into a groove, so it's a simple DIY job.

## 3. Make sure the door closes by itself
• Level: Raise the front feet slightly so the fridge tilts back a touch. Open the freezer door halfway and let go; it should swing shut.
• Alignment: Check from the side whether the door sits flush. A sagging door (often worse when heavy) can lift away at the bottom. Tightening the bottom hinge screws can fix it.

## 4. Check the bottom drawer itself
• Look for cracks, warping, or a broken front, and make sure it's sitting fully back.
• Make sure nothing is overfilled or sticking out.

## 5. Habits that make it worse
• Thermostat on max or "fast freeze" left on
• Putting warm food in
• The door being opened a lot or left ajar (kids are a classic cause!)

Quick way to tell if you've fixed it: After defrosting, check after a week. A thin, even frost is normal for manual defrost. Thick frost appearing at the front again means air's still getting in, so the seal or door alignment needs another look.

did the paper test, slides straight out at the bottom corner, grips everywhere else. bottom corner of the seal is split about 5cm and the hinge side bit is flattened. door looks straight and its level. is it push in or screwed? what do i search for to get a new one

Great, that confirms it. The split corner is your leak, and it's a straightforward DIY fix.

## Push-in or screwed?
Most modern Indesit fridge freezers have push-in seals. The seal has a ridged "arrow" strip that presses into a groove in the door liner. Some older models are screw-fixed.

To check: Open the door, peel back the inner lip of the seal (the side facing the inside of the freezer), and look underneath.
• Smooth groove, no screws → push-in. Grip the old seal at a corner and pull firmly; it'll come out.
• Row of screws → screw-fixed. Loosen the screws (you don't usually need to remove them fully), pull the old seal out, slide the new one in, and retighten.

## Finding the right seal
1. Get the model number from the rating plate, usually inside the fridge section on the side wall near the salad drawer. It'll look something like IBD 5515 W 1. Also note the service/product number (often a 12-digit number starting with 8 or 85) since that pins down the exact version.
2. Search for: `Indesit [model number] freezer door seal` (or "freezer door gasket").
3. Make sure it's the freezer seal, not the fridge one. They're different sizes.

Where to buy: Indesit's official spares site, eSpares, Partmaster, or PartsCentre. Enter your model number and it'll list the correct seal. Avoid cheap "universal" seals; they rarely fit well.

## Fitting tips
• New seals arrive folded and kinked. Soak in warm water or warm with a hairdryer on low to soften and straighten it before fitting.
• Start at the corners, then push the rest in with your thumbs.
• Close the door and leave it shut for a few hours to let the seal settle.
• Re-do the paper test. If any spot is still loose, warm it with a hairdryer and close the door again.

## In the meantime
Defrost again before fitting the new seal so the bottom drawer sits fully back. Until the part arrives, keep door openings to a minimum and check the bottom drawer is pushed fully home each time. A temporary bit of tape over the split won't seal properly, so don't rely on it.
